preamble: Total assimilation of the coda tap [ɾ] to a following [f], giving a geminate [ff]; the tap also loses its voicing. In western Cuban Spanish (the provinces from Pinar del Río to Matanzas and Cienfuegos, including Havana, plus the municipalities of Corralillo and Trinidad), coda /ɾ/ and coda /l/ merge and assimilate to the next consonant; before /f/ both surface as [f], so huérfano is pronounced hue[ff]ano, like alfiler a[ff]iler. The unassimilated pronunciations remain more common. The voicing of the first element is described differently: Goodgall de Pruna (1970) and Santana Cepero (2006) report [ff], and the acoustic study of Ruiz Hernández and Miyares Bermúdez (1984) found the first element voiced before /p/, /t/ and /k/ but not before /f/, while Costa Sánchez (1984) and Guitart (1978, 2004) describe a voiced [vf] (all as summarized by Arias 2019). Across word boundaries Arias, following Guitart's description, gives [vf] (saca[vf]ardos 'sacar fardos').
phoneticEffects: Total Assimilation, Regressive Assimilation, Gemination, Devoicing

examples.note: Arias (2019) lists it beside alfiler a[ff]iler from coda /l/; the Caribbean Spanish Wikipedia page repeats both. The sources consulted give only this one example transcribed [ff]; across word boundaries Arias, following Guitart, writes [vf] (saca[vf]ardos 'sacar fardos', anima[vf]iero 'animar fiero'), and notes that the different transcriptions follow different descriptions, not different pronunciations.

sources: Arias Cabal, Á. (2019). Fonética y fonología de las consonantes geminadas en el español de Cuba. Moenia, 25, 465–497. https://revistas.usc.gal/index.php/moenia/article/view/6474
